notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Ruth 4. The traditional-reading section (part 1) is well covered, and there is a fair amount of modern scholarship. Parts 2 and 3 are thin: my research tool hit its usage limit partway through. Several pages came only as search excerpts, not full reads, and I couldn't search the denominational, Catholic, Orthodox or popular-teaching sites at all. Gaps are marked where they come up.

Two cautions:
- The "High Points" section at the top of the enduringword.com page says it is an AI-generated summary of Guzik. I've marked points that come only from that summary.
- Biblehub's verse pages (e.g. …/ruth/4-1.htm) mix many commentators together. I name a commentator only where the excerpt made clear who was writing.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Boaz went to the gate, which worked as both courthouse and public meeting place, so the matter would be settled properly and in public. (AI summary) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-4/
- Guzik: Boaz meant to take the nearer kinsman by surprise, which gave him an advantage. The Hebrew greeting means roughly "Mr. So-and-so." The writer leaves the man unnamed because he wasn't worthy of the honour, having refused his duty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-4/
- NET note: *peloni almoni* isn't a name. It's an idiom meaning "a certain one," used when a speaker wants to stay vague (cf. 1 Sam 21:3; 2 Kgs 6:8). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rut&chapter=4
- Gill: the "behold" points to God's providence. The man happened to pass by just as Boaz sat waiting, perhaps on his way to his own field. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ruth/4.htm
- One commentator on the biblehub 4:1 page says Boaz surely knew and used the man's name. The writer left it out in contempt, as a fitting penalty: the man who wouldn't keep his brother's name alive lost his own. Another says nothing is known of him except that he turned down an offer that would have made him an ancestor of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ruth/4-1.htm
- Cambridge Bible: Boaz "went up" from the threshing floor because Bethlehem sits on two knolls, and the gate was where family law was handled (Deut 25:7). Pulpit: the town stands on a ridge, and Boaz sat on the stone benches at the gate. Keil & Delitzsch read "went up" as going up to the place of justice, not as a physical climb. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ruth/4-1.htm
- Precept Austin calls the timing a "divine coincidence." It quotes Butler: providence comes to those who are quick to do their duty, as Boaz was. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_41-10
- Bible.org: the open, daylight court process contrasts with Naomi's secret plan the night before. https://bible.org/seriespage/4-redeemed-ruth-4

**v. 2**
- JFB: two or three witnesses usually sufficed, but for weighty matters such as marriage, divorce and property transfers the Jewish practice was ten (1 Kgs 21:8). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rth/Rth_004.cfm
- Gill: the elders were officers, not just old men, and ten made a quorum for legal business. Jewish writers drew from this that a wedding blessing needs at least ten present. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ruth/4.htm
- The Gospel Coalition (TGC) commentary: the ten acted as a judicial quorum. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: the elders gave time to two poor widows, an early example of a community publicly caring for the weak. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ruth-4.html

**v. 3**
- Guzik: the kinsman-redeemer's duty included keeping land allotted to a clan within that clan. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-4/
- TGC: Naomi faced poverty and planned to sell. Land couldn't be sold permanently and had to be redeemed by the clan (Lev 25:23–24). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/
- JFB: Naomi was only thinking of selling. Boaz mentioned her alone, partly because she ran the negotiations and partly because naming Ruth would have hinted at the marriage duty too early. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rth/Rth_004.cfm
- NET note (following Bush): Naomi probably wasn't selling the land itself. She was giving up her right to redeem and use it, perhaps in return for support. This assumes Elimelech sold it before going to Moab. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rut&chapter=4
- Keil & Delitzsch: Naomi was lawfully entitled to sell. Since the field should have passed to her sons, it was as much Ruth's property as Naomi's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ruth/4-4.htm
- Expositor's Bible: Elimelech had probably borrowed against the field before leaving. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/ruth/4.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: put to him as a simple land deal, the kinsman agreed at once. Boaz knew what he was doing and stayed in control. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-4/
- Gill: the kinsman probably liked the land, which may have bordered his own, and expected a good price from a widow who had to sell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ruth/4.htm
- NET: the Hebrew actually reads "if *he* will not redeem." Most versions change it to "you," but Boaz may briefly be speaking to the witnesses (Sasson). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rut&chapter=4 The Homiletical Commentary notes the same variant and says Keil and others support the usual reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ruth-4.html
- The Bible Knowledge Commentary (quoted by Precept Austin): the property seems to have passed to Mahlon, which brought Ruth into the redemption duty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_41-10

**v. 5**
- Guzik: Boaz's surprise. It was a package deal covering both the property and the family line. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-4/
- Gill: no law required the marriage. It seems to have been a condition Naomi attached to the sale, out of care for Ruth and to keep her son's name alive (Deut 25:5). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ruth/4.htm
- The Wycliffe Bible Commentary (quoted by Precept Austin): the redeemer wouldn't keep the land himself. He would hold it in trust for his son by Ruth, who would inherit Mahlon's name and estate. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_41-10
- NET text note: the written Hebrew says "*I* acquire Ruth," while the marginal reading says "*you* [must] acquire." NET thinks the marginal reading is original; the REB follows the "I" reading. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Rut+4%3A5%2C9-10
- NET study note: in 3:13 Boaz treats the marriage as optional, but here it is a required package. Because the deal was public, the kinsman would lose face if he took the land and refused Ruth. Either way Ruth would be cared for. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rut&chapter=4

**v. 6**
- Gill: the Targum says he already had a wife, and Josephus says a wife and children. More heirs would shrink and split his estate, the field would go to Ruth's firstborn, and he might have to support Naomi too. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ruth/4.htm
- NET: it isn't entirely clear how this would ruin his inheritance. Perhaps his other children's shares would shrink (Hubbard). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rut&chapter=4
- The idea that he probably already had grown sons appears only in enduringword's AI summary. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-4/
- Matthew Henry–style application on the biblehub page: many people speak well of religion but won't commit to it, for fear of "marring their own inheritance" in this world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ruth/4-1.htm
- Homiletical Commentary: he is a type of the wavering worldly man, keen on the land and reluctant about the widow. His name is lost while Boaz's is honoured. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ruth-4.html

**vv. 7–8**
- Guzik: Deut 25:5–10 describes the sandal and the widow spitting in the man's face. Here no dishonour was involved, so only the sandal part was used. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-4/
- Clarke and JFB agree the shaming part was left out because the man had a reasonable excuse, or because he didn't actually refuse a legal duty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ruth/4-7.html ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rth/Rth_004.cfm
- Disagreement among the older commentators:
  - Coffman and Gill say this is a custom, not the levirate law of Deut 25. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ruth/4-7.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ruth/4.htm
  - One excerpt on the biblehub 4:7 page says the rite differs from Deut 25:9 because it is a general custom, not a divine command. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ruth/4-7.htm
- What the sandal meant:
  - One excerpt on the 4:7 page: the man gave up the right to walk on the land as its owner. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ruth/4-7.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch: property was claimed by treading on it, so handing over the shoe transferred ownership. The word "formerly" shows the custom had died out by the time the book was written. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ruth/4-7.htm
  - Constable: the practice links to verses about standing on land (Gen 13:17; Josh 1:3). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ruth-4.html
  - The IVP Background Commentary (quoted by Precept Austin) says sandals worked as a "moveable title" to land. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_46-10
- Who gave the sandal to whom?
  - Gill: the text doesn't say whether the kinsman or Boaz gave the shoe, and Jewish writers disagree. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ruth/4.htm
  - The Targum has Boaz drawing off his right-hand glove (Gill and Pulpit). Pulpit notes the German *Handschuh* ("hand-shoe"). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ruth-4.html
  - NET: the Greek translation (LXX) adds "and gave it to him." This may be a clarifying addition or a scribal slip. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rut&chapter=4
  - Pulpit (cited by Coffman) says Boaz politely returned the shoe afterwards. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ruth/4-8.html
- Expositor's Bible: the writer praises the simple village justice of an earlier age, quietly contrasting it with the pomp of the later monarchy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/ruth/4.htm

**v. 9**
- JFB: Chilion's widow, Orpah, was ignored. Staying in Moab meant she had remarried or given up her claim. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rth/Rth_004.cfm
- Bible.org: Boaz redeemed Chilion's share as well as Mahlon's, so all of Elimelech's estate. https://bible.org/seriespage/4-redeemed-ruth-4
- Biblical Illustrator: everything now rested on Boaz's ability and faithfulness, a picture of the hope resting on Christ as Redeemer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ruth-4.html

**v. 10**
- Guzik: Ruth seemed to give up her best hope of marriage by leaving Moab, but because she put God first she received more than she imagined. "You are witnesses" shows why a public wedding recognized by civil authorities matters. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-4/
- Gill: marrying a Moabite wasn't wrong, because Ruth had converted. Jewish teaching applied Deut 23:3 to Moabite men, not women. The "name" was kept alive through the inheritance, not by naming the son, since Obed is always called Boaz's son. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ruth/4.htm
- Bible.org: the Hebrew word "name" appears seven times in the chapter, yet the nearer kinsman's name is never given. https://bible.org/seriespage/4-redeemed-ruth-4

**v. 11**
- JFB: this was the usual wedding blessing. There were no signed deeds; the public ceremony was the security. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rth/Rth_004.cfm
- TGC: Rachel and Leah, with their maids, bore Jacob's twelve sons and so "built up the house of Israel." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ruth/
- NET: the phrase literally "do strength" is translated four ways: become wealthy, gain standing, have children, or do a worthy deed. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rut&chapter=4
- Pulpit: it echoes the word used of Boaz in 2:1 and 3:11, meaning "act the part of a strong, worthy man." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ruth-4.html

**v. 12**
- JFB: Perez was the ancestor of Bethlehem's people and head of one of Judah's five clans. The wish is for Boaz's house to be as honourable and as large as his. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rth/Rth_004.cfm
- NET: the closing genealogy shows the blessing came true; Boaz's line became like Perez's. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rut&chapter=4

**v. 13**
- Guzik: Israel never took children for granted; the son was a sign of God's blessing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-4/
- Gill: the marriage had no rites beyond those described here; later Jewish wedding ceremonies didn't exist yet. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ruth-4.html
- Poole: the ban on marrying Moabites applied only to those who stayed heathen, and Ruth was a sincere convert. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ruth/4-13.htm
- Gotquestions.org: Deut 23:3 bans Moabites from naturalization but doesn't mention marriage. Jewish law applied it to men only (Mishnah Yevamot 8:3), Ruth was a convert, and God blessed the marriage. https://www.gotquestions.org/Boaz-Ruth-and-the-Law.html
- Biblehub's Q&A: the ban targeted continuing hostility; true conversion, as in Ruth 1:16, opened a way in. https://biblehub.com/q/how_does_ruth_fit_deut._23_3's_exclusion.htm
- NET: the Hebrew is literally "gave her conception." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Rut&chapter=4&verse=13

**v. 14**
- NET: the "guardian/redeemer" here is the child. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Rut+4%3A13-17&theme=wiki
- Bible.org: the women gently correct Naomi; she was not "empty" after all. https://bible.org/seriespage/4-redeemed-ruth-4
- Guzik: compare Naomi's bitterness in 1:20–21. Her return to Bethlehem started all of this, and God knows what he is doing even when things look hopeless. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-4/

**v. 15**
- Gill: the grandson would restore Naomi's lost joy and support her in old age as heir to a large estate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ruth/4-15.htm
- Bibleodyssey (HarperCollins dictionary): seven sons was the ideal number. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/HarperCollinsBibleDictionary/r/ruth

**v. 16**
- NET: "nurse" means a caregiver who isn't nursing the baby (a "dry nurse"); "lap" can also be "bosom." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Rut+4%3A13-17&theme=wiki
- Pulpit Homiletics: Naomi's unselfishness toward Ruth is rewarded. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/ruth/4.htm
- Bible.org: Naomi went out "full" and came back "empty," and now her arms are full. https://bible.org/seriespage/4-redeemed-ruth-4

**v. 17**
- NET: Obed means "one who serves," perhaps looking ahead to how he would help Naomi. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Rut+4%3A13-17&theme=wiki JFB: "servant." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rth/Rth_004.cfm
- Guzik: Ruth and Boaz's Bethlehem roots are why Joseph and Mary went to Bethlehem (Luke 2:1–5). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ruth-4/

**vv. 18–22**
- Matthew Henry: the genealogy runs from Perez to David and on toward the Messiah. Ruth's place in it was her greatest honour. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rth/Rth_004.cfm
- NET: Salmah (v. 20) and Salmon (v. 21) are probably two spellings of one name. Through David and then Jesus, God's reward went far beyond the lifetimes of Ruth and Boaz. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Rut&chapter=4
- Pulpit Homiletics: the line helped commend Jesus to the Jewish people and confirmed prophecy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/ruth/4.htm
- Bibleodyssey: Ruth also appears in Matthew's genealogy, which names Rahab as the mother of Boaz (Matt 1:5). https://www.bibleodyssey.org/HarperCollinsBibleDictionary/r/ruth

**Whole chapter: Christ as the Redeemer (a reading shared across the sources)**
- Homiletical Commentary: Christ is our kinsman, which is why he took on flesh. Quoting Wordsworth, Christ is the Redeemer "whose shoe is never drawn off." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ruth-4.html
- Matthew Henry: Christ redeemed the forfeited inheritance at great cost and took to himself people who were foreigners, like Ruth. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rth/Rth_004.cfm
- Precept Austin quotes several writers:
  - redemption is a legal matter, like justification;
  - the nearer kinsman "is the law," which can't redeem;
  - Ruth stands for the Church, the treasure in the field (Matt 13:44). https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_41-10

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I couldn't search the denominational sites (desiringgod, ligonier, lcms, 1517, seedbed, Wesley's notes), so I can't report differences in each tradition's own words. The only contrast in what I read is between two older commentaries. Neither names a denomination.
- **Precept Austin**, quoting an unnamed writer: Christ, like Boaz, is "not free to move" for you until you claim him as Redeemer; you must reach out and receive him by faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ruth_41-10
- **The Biblical Illustrator**, on vv. 1–5: Boaz arranged everything without Ruth knowing, just as Christ's work was planned and finished "without your counsel," which it calls "sovereign grace." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ruth-4.html

These touch the classic Reformed versus Arminian debate over how salvation begins: God's choice first, or the believer's response. But I couldn't tie either to a tradition's own teachers.

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- Scholars disagree on whether Ruth 4 is levirate marriage at all. Boaz isn't Ruth's brother-in-law, and the genealogy doesn't count Obed as Mahlon's son. The article suggests the real goal of levirate may have been protecting widows, a goal the women in these stories pursued more than the men did. https://helpmewithbiblestudy.bibleodyssey.org/articles/levirate-marriage/
- Ruth decides nothing in the official scene at the gate and is left out of the male genealogy. Even so, the author argues she is the book's real hero. Some scholars think the book protests Ezra's ban on foreign wives (Ezra 9–10; Neh 13). https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/ruth/
- One article reads Ruth as a fairy tale. "Mr. So-and-So" is a rhyming nonsense name, and Boaz beats him with clever words. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/ruth-as-a-fairy-tale/
- The NET notes above on the Hebrew text in vv. 4–5 and the sandal in v. 8 also belong here.

**Catholic and Orthodox readings; prosperity, word of faith and hyper-grace teaching:** not found. I couldn't search newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, and found nothing on the popular modern teachings.
